common_name: Peach Flambe Heuchera (Peach Flambe Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, siting the plant where it gets some morning sun to intensify its warm coloring without scorching the foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, siting the plant where it gets some morning sun to intensify its warm coloring without scorching the foliage. Peach Flambe produces ruffled, rounded leaves that emerge glowing peach-orange and shift through amber and copper tones as the season progresses, brightest in cool spring and fall weather. Small bell-shaped flowers appear on wiry stems in early summer, but the plant is grown mainly as a season-long foliage accent along a shaded path or border edge. Like most modern heuchera hybrids it benefits from division every three to four years to prevent the woody crown from heaving out of the soil.

common_name: Midnight Bayou Heuchera (Midnight Bayou Coral Bells)

planting.note: Install divisions in partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil, where the deeply lobed, glossy foliage can be appreciated up close along a path or container edge.

directions: Install divisions in partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil, where the deeply lobed, glossy foliage can be appreciated up close along a path or container edge. Midnight Bayou is a vigorous, spreading hybrid with lustrous purple-black leaves overlaid with a silvery sheen and prominent red-purple veining, a striking contrast plant among lighter-colored hostas and ferns. Wiry, pinkish-white flower stems rise above the foliage in early summer, though the plant's main appeal is its season-long dark, glossy leaf color. It tolerates heavier soils and more sun than many heuchera cultivars, provided moisture is consistent.

common_name: Silver Heart Brunnera (Silver Heart Siberian Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly cool and moist.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly cool and moist. Silver Heart carries broad, heart-shaped leaves that are almost entirely silvered, interrupted only by fine dark-green veining, giving it one of the brightest all-silver effects among brunnera cultivars, topped in early spring by sprays of small sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers. It forms a tidy, non-invasive clump that lights up a dim woodland corner from spring through frost. Established plantings rarely need division and tolerate deep shade better than most variegated shade perennials.

Opal is prized for its unusually soft, pale ice-blue flowers, a subtler and cooler tone than the typical pink-to-blue pulmonaria palette, held above lightly spotted, softly hairy green leaves in earliest spring. It provides one of the season's first nectar sources for emerging bumblebees and pairs elegantly with hellebores and early daffodils. Shear off tattered summer foliage to encourage a fresh, cleaner-looking flush of leaves for the rest of the season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where its narrow, heavily silver-spotted leaves can spread into a dense, weed-suppressing mat.

This long-established hybrid between Pulmonaria longifolia and P. saccharata is valued for clear sky-blue flowers held well above the foliage in early spring and for being noticeably more vigorous and heat-tolerant than many older lungwort selections. It has held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliability and garden performance. Named for Pacific Northwest plantsman Roy Davidson, it makes an excellent long-lived groundcover beneath deciduous shrubs.
